newsitem.title: GERMANY: Young CDU leader wants looser German EMU stand.
newsitem.headline: Young CDU leader wants looser German EMU stand.

text.p: A leading young ally of Chancellor Helmut Kohl urged the cash-strapped German government on Friday to calm down and take a more relaxed view of the Maastricht treaty's three percent budget deficit target.

Peter Mueller, head of Kohl's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in Saar state bordering France, said Bonn's decision to revalue Bundesbank gold to qualify for Europe's monetary union (EMU) made the government look "out of breath" and "hectic."
Kohl's 14-year-old centre-right coalition has lost its reputation for economic competence and would have to regain it fast if it wanted to win reelection next year, he said.

The statement by Mueller, 41, a prominent figure in the "wild youngsters" generation of up-and-coming CDU leaders, brought out into the open some of the doubts in the party ranks about Finance Minister Theo Waigel's hard EMU line.
"I think we should talk again about which deficit criteria the Maastricht treaty provides for," said Mueller, referring to the three percent deficit-to-GDP target in the treaty.
"This is the source of the problem. We have manoeuvered ourselves into a situation that the treaty does not require.
"A reasonable look at the Maastricht treaty shows there is no obligation to have a deficit of 3.0 percent. There is room to manoeuvre and we should use it."
The business daily Handelsblatt concurred in its first editorial on the Bundesbank reserves row.

"Now it's not a question of keeping to a certain number at a certain time come hell or high water," it wrote. "It is more important to show the will to conduct a sustainable and solid financial policy without cheating -- that will create credibility for the euro."
In another interview, CDU secretary general Peter Hintze defended Waigel's plan and said he should not step down as the opposition Social Democrats and Greens have demanded.

Waigel, who opted for the gold plan to help fill yawning gaps in his 1997 budget without going over the three percent target, has long insisted only a strict interpretation of the treaty would ensure that the euro is stable.

While he claims voters would not accept anything less rigid, Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke suggested on Wednesday Waigel takes such a tough line because of pressure from his main rival, Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber.

Stoiber, who wants to take the leadership of the Christian Social Union (CSU) party away from Waigel, has insisted on the toughest possible interpretation to focus popular discontent with EMU onto his rival, political sources say.

Mueller said the Bonn-Bundesbank showdown that flared up after the bank bluntly rejected Waigel's revaluation plan was "an annoyance" that should not force either side to resign. "I don't think anyone has to lose face," he said.
"As for revaluing the gold reserves, one has to ask whether 1997 is the right year for this. Maybe it would be better to wait until the European Central Bank is established," he added.

Mueller, who with other younger CDU provincial leaders has already been tipped to play a larger role in the post-Kohl era, said the gold feud had harmed the party's image as it prepares for a tough campaign for the election in September 1998.
"At the moment, things aren't going very well," he said. "If we want to win the general election, we have to see to it that the political scene calms down.

"Financial policy was always a strong suit of the CDU. Competence in this issue is a prerequisite for keeping our majority. We have to win back this competence very quickly by making long-term policies and not starting up a new debate after every tax estimate. Then we have a good chance to win the next election."

CDU officials said on Thursday that Kohl was taking an enormous gamble by opting for the controversial step of imposing his political will on the popular Bundesbank to achieve a goal that does not have wide voter support.
Over two-thirds of Germans do not want to give up their strong mark, but pollsters have said until now they trusted Kohl to ensure the euro would be just as stable.
"We'll have to see now whether this is still the case," one party official said.

In April, two CDU backbenchers in Bonn criticised Waigel's fixation on meeting the deficit target precisely, but their letter could not get a public debate going against the closed ranks of Waigel's supporters in the coalition leadership.

"We have lost the political leadership and allowed the criteria to be limited to the reference values," Armin Laschet and Franz Peter Basten wrote. "We must now stop falsifying this three percent into a litmus test of stable money."
Kohl shies away from numbers, preferring to say Bonn will meet the criteria on time and to keep up the pressure on other EU members by making clear he wants to see the project through.
